articles.title: Oracle layoffs: Employees receive ‘6am job cuts’ email from “Oracle leadership” again, saying: We are sharing some…
articles.summary: Tech News News: Oracle began cutting jobs again on September 14, and the people affected found out in almost exactly the sequence they did in March. Federated logins .
articles.body: Oracle began cutting jobs again on September 14, and the people affected found out in almost exactly the sequence they did in March. Federated logins stopped working at around 4am Eastern. Slack sessions dropped out in a rolling wave between 5am and 5.30am. Badges failed at office gates. Then, at 6am local time, an email from "Oracle Leadership" arrived, according to three impacted employees and a copy of the notification seen by Business Insider, carrying the line staff had been bracing for since August: "We are sharing some difficult news regarding your position." The role had been eliminated as part of a broader organisational change, and the same day was the last working day.The round had been expected since mid-August, when managers were asked to submit lists of employees whose jobs were going, with payroll to come down early in Oracle's second fiscal quarter. Oracle has not commented. On Reddit's r/employeesOfOracle forum, where a thread crossed 300 comments within hours, workers watched Slack membership fall by roughly 3,000 to 4,000 through the morning and posted their orgs one after another: OCI security, CI/CD, enterprise engineering, observability, executive escalations, Fusion, NetSuite sales, Customer Success Services, Oracle Health, EPM, HR Technology, data centre compliance, and the Stargate site in Abilene, Texas.Performance ratings did not protect Oracle employees from the 6am layoff emailOne detail ran through nearly every post. The people cut on Monday were not the ones with poor reviews. An IC4 in HR Technology reported four straight ratings of four and a five before being let go. A four-year OCI employee said he had never scored below "meets expectations". A QA engineer with 24 years of service got the same email. One employee at the Abilene site had started on February 2. Several said the only shift was a rating that slipped a notch this cycle, after their team was folded under OCI.Severance information was slow to follow. Many lost email and VPN access before any document arrived, leaving them waiting on a message to a personal address they had not yet been able to submit. One employee in the database org with four years of service reported seven weeks of severance.Oracle layoffs are expected to reach the India Development Centre nextThe US wave appeared to finish within a few hours. India is expected to follow, as it did in March, with employees estimating cuts of 3,000 to 4,000 across the India Development Centre and around 30% in customer support. EMEA is expected to come last, and some European cases from the March round remain open. Severance in India in that earlier wave broadly followed the N+2 formula, with unvested restricted stock forfeited on exit.Oracle's restructuring bill has grown to $2.8 billion as data centre spending climbsThe financial backdrop shifted three days earlier. In a filing on Friday, Oracle said restructuring costs would rise by about $700 million, taking the expected cost of its fiscal 2026 plan to roughly $2.8 billion, and tied part of the plan to the adoption of AI across some functions. First-quarter capital expenditure came in at $28.5 billion against $8.5 billion a year earlier, and the fiscal 2027 forecast stayed at $90 billion to $95 billion. Free cash flow ran to negative $5.40 billion.Headcount had already fallen by 21,000 in the fiscal year that ended May 31, leaving about 141,000 employees before Monday. Revenue backlog grew by $26 billion to $664 billion, the figure Oracle keeps pointing to as proof the spending works. The stock is down about 23% this year. Since August, employees had traded dates on Reddit: September 1, then the 15th, then the 30th. None of them was announced. The one that counted arrived as a login failure at 4am.Read the layoff email employees recieved from Oracle leadership:We are sharing some difficult news regarding your position.After careful consideration of Oracle's current business needs, we have made the decision to eliminate your role as part of a broader organizational change. As a result, today is your last working day.We are grateful for your dedication, hard work, and the impact you have made during your time with us.After signing your termination paperwork, you will be eligible to receive a severance package subject to the terms and conditions of the severance plan. You will receive an email from DocuSign to your Oracle email address with details on your severance and termination date.Immediate Action RequiredTo receive important follow-up information, including FAQs and separation documents to help you through this transition, you must provide a personal email address.Please click here to submit a personal email address immediately. If you make a submission error, please re-submit a new form. Please Note: The personal email address will only be used for correspondence regarding separation-related information and severance agreements.Access to your computer, email, voicemail, and files will be deactivated soon, and you will be unable to log into your computer. As a reminder, you are prohibited from downloading, copying or retaining (including emailing yourself any Oracle confidential information.Thank you for your contributions to our organization. If you have additional questions, please reach out to the HR team via the Ask HR page…Oracle Leadership.Get the latest technology news and updates. Download the TOI App.

articles.title: Can a party be leftist and Zionist?
articles.summary: No, it cannot. But the concept of leftist Zionism is still being pushed to cover up its racist, colonial nature.
articles.body:
Ahead of Israel’s October 27 elections, Israel’s Young Democrats, the youth wing of the newly formed Democrats party, are seeking foreign allies. They recently announced a joint campaign with the Young Greens of Austria to support “progressive voices on the ground and work with them towards a sustainable peace”.

Meanwhile, another youth group described as “leftist”, Hamahanot Haolim (the Ascending Camps), is exploring plans to build a new kibbutz in the occupied West Bank, near Jericho.

When questioned about the impact on the Palestinian population, the group’s director, Ilan Gazit, explained that since Israeli settlements are being built regardless, “the left” should make sure it is Israeli “leftists”, not far-right settlers, who populate them. “We aren’t ashamed of this, and we aren’t hiding it,” he said.

These two youth movements and their foreign sympathisers appear to treat “leftist Zionism” as a coherent political identity. But can a party, a movement, or an individual be both leftist and Zionist?

The short answer, from a Palestinian and anti‑colonial perspective, is no. So why is it touted in Israel and beyond as a legitimate ideological belief? Because it is a political technology designed to shield Zionism from any critique while preserving the structures of oppression.

The question about the viability of “leftist Zionism” is not new. Zionism emerged as an organised Jewish nationalist movement in Europe in the 19th century. At its core was the aim of establishing a Jewish national home, an idea shaped by European nationalism, European anti-Semitism, and colonial expansion.

Its early political architects advanced two connected projects: redefining Judaism as a national identity and colonising Palestine. Theodor Herzl, a Hungarian Jewish journalist who is seen as the founder of Zionism, was motivated not by religious zeal, as he espoused secularism, but by the growing anti-Semitism in Europe.

After Herzl’s death in 1904, leftist ideas entered the movement as various socialist factions rose to dominance within the World Zionist Organization and in early settler communities in Palestine itself.

But these leftist elements were not driven by a genuine commitment to class-based struggle and internationalism. Rather, they used a socialist vocabulary to justify a settler-colonial nation-building project, carried out through kibbutzim, labour unions, and diplomacy.

Whatever position early Zionists staked out on the political spectrum, what the movement ultimately produced — the state of Israel — was in direct contradiction with the anti-colonial, anti-racist politics the left was supposed to stand for.

In 1975, the United Nations General Assembly acknowledged this by adopting Resolution 3379, declaring that “Zionism is a form of racism and racial discrimination”. The resolution was revoked in 1991, after sustained pressure from Israel and its allies and in the wake of the Soviet collapse.

The debate about “leftist Zionism” continues till today. The issue is not whether individual Zionists can hold progressive views on particular social or economic questions. Some might.

The real question is whether a political project organised around building and sustaining a state premised on Jewish supremacy through ethnic cleansing, dispossession, apartheid, and now genocide can be reconciled with the left’s foundational commitments: equity, anti‑racism, decolonisation, and social justice for everyone.

When considering the historical record, it is important to note that for decades, Israel was governed by parties that would self-describe as “leftist”.

Mapai was established as a Labour Zionist party in 1930, led by David Ben-Gurion. It became the dominant force within early Zionist politics and the principal architect of the pre‑state and early institutions, including the Haganah, which carried out various terrorist attacks and massacres against the Palestinians.

Mapai governed Israel well into the 1960s, giving way to the Labour Party, which dominated Israeli politics until the 1990s.

Labour Zionism spoke the language of workers’ solidarity while building institutions that excluded Palestinians by design.

The Histadrut, Israel’s dominant trade‑union confederation, was founded in 1920 as an instrument of the Zionist “conquest of labour”: a project designed to build Jewish settlements by systematically displacing Palestinian workers from the economy and reducing dependence on Indigenous labour. After 1948, this exclusion was institutionalised: Palestinian workers were either barred from membership outright or confined to second‑class status for decades, denied voting rights and meaningful representation even as they paid union fees.

Today, even when on paper Palestinians should have the same rights as Jewish Israeli workers, in practice, they do not. Collective bargaining agreements in key sectors, such as construction , are consistently not applied to them because their employment is rendered unstable, informal, and “temporary” by design. In this way, the Histadrut functions less as a defender of workers’ rights and more as a key actor in reproducing a settler‑colonial order that segregates, exploits, and disempowers Palestinian labour.

The school system set up by early Labour governments functioned as an instrument of ideological formation: forging Jewish national consciousness while erasing Palestinian presence, and recasting settlement as national redemption rather than colonisation.

The kibbutz and moshav movements, the flagship institutions of Labour Zionism, were central to the project of land theft and displacement. Many kibbutzim, due to their location, served as staging grounds for Haganah operations in 1948, including the depopulation of nearby Palestinian villages, making the settlement map itself part of the operational infrastructure of the Nakba.

Falling into the left-right Zionist trap

Despite the long historical record of crimes committed by Mapai and Labour governments against the Palestinians, many leftists in the West continue to fall for the “leftist” label within the context of Israeli politics. They appear to believe that what is happening in Palestine could be solely blamed on Israel’s right-wing political forces led by Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu.

Campaigns like that of the Young Greens of Austria and Israel’s Young Democrats seemingly reinforce this misguided belief. In the end, their ultimate aim is not to amplify “progressive voices” or deliver a “just peace” to the Palestinians, but to impose a political category – “leftist Zionist” – that is, in essence, incoherent and contradictory.

The constant reference to a “far‑right Netanyahu government” does real political work. It implies that a “Zionist left” could be a credible progressive alternative, one that is capable of changing the colonial reality Palestinians live under and one that is not to blame for Israeli crimes.

That framing lets the underlying structure – Israel’s settler colonialism – off the hook, treating it as a policy choice of the Israeli far right specifically rather than the logic of Zionism itself.

Palestinians do not need political theory to see the truth. Generations of them know, in their flesh, that there is no difference between Zionism on the left and Zionism on the right when it comes to their dispossession. The occupation did not start with Netanyahu, and a change in government will not end it.

Any leftist party in Europe or beyond that wants to remain aligned with its own values has one path. It should listen to Palestinians, follow and support forces like the Green Party of England and Wales in naming Zionism for what it is: a racist, settler-colonial ideology. Not a policy to be reformed, but an ideology to be abolished.

The views expressed in this article are the author’s own and do not necessarily reflect Al Jazeera’s editorial stance.

articles.title: 4 hospitalized after crane collapses in Miami, fire rescue says
articles.summary: Four people were taken to the hospital on Monday after a crane collapsed in Brickell, fire rescue officials said.
articles.body: Four people were taken to the hospital on Monday after a crane collapsed in Brickell, fire rescue officials said. According to Miami Fire Rescue, the crane collapsed on Southeast 12th Street and Brickell Bay Drive. Video shows the downed crane, as well as vehicle next to it that caught on fire. Fire rescue said that the driver of the white SUV that caught on fire saw the crane falling, stopped her vehicle and put in reverse. The crane then landed on the SUV’s hood, which caused a fire, and the driver was able to escape by going to the back. Four people, including three construction workers, were taken to the hospital after a complex rescue operation. Two workers, ages 29 and 27, were in a construction box when the crane fell on top of it, trapping them. “It was a very complex scene with a fire that was occurring, our crews were putting out the fire and our technical rescue team working simultaneously to cut through the Conex box, the construction box, and they were able to successfully able to extricate the two victims,” Miami Fire Rescue Chief Robert Hevia. A third construction worker, the crane operator, jumped out of the crane as it was tipping over. The 47-year-old crane operators, the two other constructions workers and the driver of the SUV, were then taken to the hospital with minor injuries. All 18 constructions workers on the site were accounted for, Hevia said. NBC6 spoke with a resident who saw the crane collapse. “On my way home, I ran an errand at Publix, and was turning the corner in order to access my parking garage, as I entered, I heard a tremendous crash,” Christina Larden said. “I dropped everything and went down to the street and saw a car in flames. Flames were shooting up 20, 30 feet in the air.” Details on how the crane fell were not released. As crews work the incident, Brickell Bay Drive has been closed between Southeast 12th Street and 13th Street. The eastbound lanes of Northwest 17th Street at Seventh Avenue were also closed. The Occupational Safety and Health Administration will arrive to assess the incident.

articles.title: Jury discharged in Boris Johnson wedding plot trial
articles.summary: A jury fails to reach a verdict for Tim Speers who was accused of planning a protest at the event.
articles.body:
A jury has been discharged after failing to reach a verdict in the trial of a man accused of plotting to disrupt Boris Johnson's wedding reception.

Tim Speers, 41, allegedly carried spray paint and superglue to the Doylesford Estate in Gloucestershire on 29 July 2022, on the eve of the former prime minister and Carrie Johnson's wedding reception.

Speers, from Bude, Cornwall, denied having items with intent to cause criminal damage and said he abandoned the idea to spray "Palestine" on the lawn by the time police approached him.

The judge discharged the jury and adjourned the case at Southwark Crown Court until 29 September, when prosecutors have been told to indicate if they want a retrial.

Airport to be sold by April says council leader

Capita pension backlog leaves widows 'in tears'

During the trial, the jury heard that police stopped Speers and another man, who will stand trial at a later date, after the pair were spotted carrying cans of beer at the Cotswold estate.

They initially refused to tell police why they were there and then said they were on holiday.

Christiaan Moll, prosecuting, said police found a voice note recorded by Speers the day before his arrest in which he said he had been asked by two Palestine Action activists to take part in "action" and he "agreed to do it".

The jury - which began deliberations on Friday - had sent the judge a series of notes that said they were "stuck" and divided on the verdict.

The Johnsons were married in a private ceremony at Westminster Cathedral in May 2021.

They hosted their wedding celebrations at Daylesford House on 30 July the following year, setting up marquees and hay bales in the grounds.

articles.title: California Democrat faces ouster call after her former professor tells crowd to 'f--- up' ICE agent
articles.summary: Video shows professor Melina Abdullah naming an ICE agent and sharing his hotel address before Sasha Renée Pérez took the stage at the summit.
articles.body: California state Sen. Sasha Renée Pérez, D-Pasadena, faced a call Sunday to lose her chairmanship of the Senate Education Committee after appearing at an immigration summit alongside a former professor who repeatedly told the crowd to "f--- up" a named ICE agent. Video from last Sunday’s La Defensa Del Pueblo summit showed California State University, Los Angeles, professor Melina Abdullah identifying an ICE agent, saying he "may be staying" at a local Hilton Garden Inn and giving the crowd the hotel’s street address. Abdullah repeatedly said to "f--- him up" before later explaining the phrase could include exposing immigration agents or making them uncomfortable. She also encouraged attendees to "study guerrilla warfare." CALIFORNIA BILL WOULD LET ILLEGAL IMMIGRANT PROFESSORS KEEP TEACHING US STUDENTS REMOTELY California Republican Party delegate and attorney Elizabeth Barcohana told Fox News Digital on Sunday that Pérez should no longer lead the Senate committee responsible for education policy. "I believe Pérez should be removed as chair of education committee," Barcohana said. Abdullah is a professor of Pan-African Studies at Cal State LA and a leader of Black Lives Matter Los Angeles. The university describes Abdullah as a "scholar-activist" who views her academic role as connected to broader activist movements. After Abdullah’s remarks, Pérez took the microphone and referenced their former professor-student relationship. "Y’all, it’s really hard to follow up my old college professor, Dr. Melina Abdullah… It’s such an honor to share space with you and to be able to sit next to you here," Pérez said. ANTI-ICE WALKOUT EXPOSES HOW SCHOOL DISTRICT 'FAILED' PARENTS, RISKED STUDENT SAFETY: 'BROKEN MY TRUST' Perez responded last week to suggestions that she was smiling at the professor's remarks, saying the video was edited. "I unequivocally condemn violence in all its forms, regardless of who uses it or whom it targets. I do not support, endorse, or condone violence against anyone, and my silence during another panelist’s remarks must never be misrepresented as agreement. Each speaker is responsible for their own words. A highly edited video circulating online falsely suggests I was smiling in response to violent remarks directed toward an ICE agent. The full video makes clear that my reaction was to separate comments about the courage of young people. Any suggestion that I share, endorse, or condone violence is false," Perez said, according to Los Angeles County Politics. "I have consistently opposed the federal government’s cruel immigration enforcement practices while also unequivocally opposing violence in all forms including violence by government agents that took the life of Keith Porter Jr. and Lorenzo Salgado Araujo and violence by political extremists that took the life of Charlie Kirk. Political disagreement is not a license for racism, intimidation, or violence. I will continue to fight for civil rights through lawful, democratic action, and I will never condone violence." Pérez earned degrees in political science and economics from Cal State LA before entering public service. Barcohana also linked Pérez’s appearance alongside Abdullah to the senator’s role as chair of the Senate Education Committee and her record on immigration enforcement at California schools. In a post about the summit, Barcohana specifically pointed to legislation Pérez authored requiring schools to issue alerts about immigration enforcement activity. "Most relevant to this weekend’s summit, Pérez authored the bill that would turn California schools into participants in ICE resistance, rather than a neutral and safe learning environment for children," Barcohana said on X. "As Chair of the Education committee, Pérez saw to it that the antisemitism bill in the California legislature was rendered completely useless to its intended purpose of protecting Jewish students from harassment, discrimination, and intimidation. The bill was necessary because antisemitic incidents have increased over 600% in California K-12 schools." DOJ DEMANDS SANCTUARY STATES END 'BLATANTLY UNLAWFUL' ANTI-ICE POLICY AS A MATTER OF LIFE AND DEATH Pérez authored SB 98, the Sending Alerts to Families in Education, or SAFE, Act, which Gov. Gavin Newsom signed into law in September 2025. The law requires K-12 schools and higher education institutions to notify campus communities when immigration enforcement authorities are present on campus. When Pérez introduced the bill in January 2025, her office said the proposal came in response to the Trump administration eliminating Biden-era guidance limiting immigration enforcement in certain "protected areas," including schools. Pérez framed the measure as a response to concerns among immigrant students and parents about federal enforcement. "The Trump administration has made clear that no place is safe from mass deportations. Students and parents are rightfully scared," Pérez said. "We will not be silent." CLICK HERE FOR MORE COVERAGE OF MEDIA AND CULTURE Newsom signed the legislation with an urgency clause, putting it into effect immediately. Pérez’s office has described the notifications as similar to warning systems used for other campus emergencies. Pérez also criticized federal immigration authorities in 2025 when responding to plans for immigration enforcement agencies to participate in a Cal Poly Pomona career fair. "ICE should have no place on our campuses," Pérez said. CLICK HERE TO DOWNLOAD THE FOX NEWS APP A DHS spokesperson told Fox News Digital, "Governor Newsom continues to refuse to do his job to protect his citizens from illegal alien crime and instead chooses to smear our law enforcement." "California politicians should focus on educating students, not turning classrooms into sanctuaries for illegal aliens. SB98 is a political stunt designed to create fear, interfere with law enforcement, and shield those who have violated our nation’s law. DHS will continue enforcing the laws Congress passed, and enforcing federal law when necessary, consistent with the Constitution and all applicable legal requirements. No state law will prevent federal officers from protecting American communities." "While the media and sanctuary politicians try and spread falsehoods and demean DHS law enforcement, the men and woman of DHS are risking their lives and safety to arrest illegal criminal aliens that are victimizing Americans. Our message is clear: if you come to our country illegally, we will find you, we will arrest you, and we will deport you," the spokesperson added. Republican California state Sen. Tony Strickland also said in comments to Fox News Digital, "The most essential role of government is public safety. As a legislator, I firmly stand with the men and women who put their lives on the line every day to protect our communities. Political disagreement does not justify intimidation or putting an officer and his family at risk. While free speech is a fundamental right, credible threats or targeted harassment must be taken seriously and investigated based on the facts and the law." Fox News Digital reached out to Pérez, Abdullah and Cal State Los Angeles for comment, but did not immediately receive a response.

articles.title: Leaders of Scotland, Wales, Northern Ireland unite for self-determination
articles.summary: Leaders of nationalist parties in Scotland, Wales and Northern Ireland say London has ‘no right’ to block democracy.
articles.body:
The leaders of the main political parties in Scotland, Wales and Northern Ireland have declared their right to “self determination” in a joint agreement signed at a rare meeting in the Welsh capital, Cardiff.

All three parties – the Scottish National Party (SNP), Plaid Cymru in Wales and the pro-Irish unity Sinn Fein in Northern Ireland – want greater autonomy and eventually independence from the UK, but have different views on issues such as referendums and timelines.

The SNP’s John Swinney, Sinn Fein’s Michelle O’Neill and Plaid Cymru’s Rhun ap Iorwerth attended in their capacity as party leaders, rather than as officials in their respective governments.

Laura McAllister from Cardiff University told Al Jazeera that the wording of the agreement was “deliberately” couched in the broader “constitutional language of self-determination”.

“This is the first time that the nations of the United Kingdom are attempting to drive the constitutional question,” she said. “They also covered some of the more practical policy areas where they may wish to share stances, such as renewable energy, relationships with Europe, economic development.”

What does the three-party joint agreement say exactly?

“Our nations have the right to self-determination. No Westminster government has the right to block democracy or undermine the principle that our people will decide their own future,” they said on Monday, referring to the UK-wide parliament in London.

“For the first time ever, people across these islands have first ministers in Scotland, in Wales and in the North of Ireland who are all committed to independence from the United Kingdom,” the memorandum of understanding continued.

“The future of our nations belongs in the European Union … For people watching across these islands – for people watching around the world – there could be no clearer sign that Westminster’s time is coming to an end.

“Momentum is behind our movements; we believe that constitutional change is coming,” the agreement said.

What has the UK PM said on pro-independence movements?

Sinn Fein wants Northern Ireland to leave the United Kingdom and join a united Ireland.

The forum happened after US President Donald Trump weighed in on a potential breakup of the UK. He told reporters that a unified Ireland would be “fantastic” during a visit to Ireland on Saturday. “Now the UK will have something to say about it … but I think it would be a great thing,” he added.

Indeed, Prime Minister Andy Burnham had something to say on Trump’s comment – that his position on Irish unification remained unchanged.

On August 27, Britain’s newly-elected leader said a referendum on Northern Ireland leaving the UK was “off the table”.

Burnham has also dashed hopes among some for a second vote on Scottish independence, saying recently that another referendum was “off limits”.

What is the legal status of the three regions?

Constitutionally, the UK has four constituent countries: England, Wales, Scotland, and Northern Ireland. Within these four jurisdictions there are three legal systems:

England and Wales have a combined legal system.

Scotland operates as a distinct legal system based on Scots law.

Northern Ireland has its own distinct, independent legal system based on English common law and its own legislation.

Power is shared in a system known as devolution, unlike in the federal system of the United States or Germany. It means power is not constitutionally divided on an equal basis between a central government and the four nations.

Elected institutions have some powers with their own legislatures and governments, but defence and foreign affairs, among other issues, remain controlled by London.

Crucially, none of the states has the right to unilaterally leave the UK.

Scotland held an independence referendum in 2014 after Westminster gave the green light. Independence was rejected by 55 percent to 45 percent. Wales similarly has no existing legal mechanism allowing the Senedd (Welsh parliament) to call an independence referendum on its own.

For Northern Ireland, the rules are different . Under the terms of the 1998 Good Friday Agreement, the British government must call a referendum if the UK secretary for Northern Ireland believes it is “likely” that a majority would vote for a united Ireland.

Has the mood for greater autonomy grown?

Recent polling points to significant, though varying, support for constitutional change.

A Survation poll found 47 percent backing Scottish independence, while a University of Liverpool survey found 36 percent in Northern Ireland would vote for Irish reunification.

In Wales, a Survation poll put support for independence at 32 percent.

“Plaid Cymru was elected with heavy emphasis on avoiding the issue of independence,” explained McAllister. “The situation in Scotland is very different” and “fundamentally” so in Northern Ireland and the Irish Republic, she added, describing Monday’s meeting as “very tactical and very strategic”.

articles.title: Trump's Green Card rule challenged by a coalition of states and local governments who call new policy 'catastrophic'
articles.summary: US News: A new Green Card rule is scheduled to come into effect on September 18, in which an officer can deny a Green Card to an applicant if they can potentia.
articles.body: A new Green Card rule is scheduled to come into effect on September 18, in which an officer can deny a Green Card to an applicant if they can potentially become a burden on the US government. With four days left for this new rule, a coalition of states and local governments Monday sued the administration over the "catastrophic" policy.The challenge, brought by two separate lawsuits, has aimed to block a policy that is set to take effect Friday. The suit filed by 22 states and the District of Columbia argued that the policy would hurt immigrant families by forcing them to either turn away from public assistance programs to meet their basic needs or risk being denied green cards in the future, the New York Times reported.It also argued that it would harm states and localities by straining emergency rooms and reducing participation in food stamps, which would drain money from local businesses that depend on the federal benefits.“Hard-working families should not be forced to go without the support they need because they fear asking for assistance will get them deported,” Letitia James, the Democratic attorney general of New York who led the suit, said in a statement.What is the new 'public charge' rule?Trump officials have said the policy, known as the “public charge” rule, is necessary to protect public resources and to restore “the basic principle that immigrants must be able to support themselves.”USCIS officers will consider the five statutory factors and any other factor relevant to assessing the alien’s likelihood at any time of becoming a public charge, including the alien’s receipt of means-tested public benefits, such as cash assistance for income maintenance, housing assistance, food stamps, financial aid for college, or any other similar benefit. For means-tested public benefits received before September 18, 2026, USCIS will only consider the alien’s receipt of public cash assistance for income maintenance and long-term institutionalization at the government’s expense. For means-tested public benefits received on or after September 18, 2026, USCIS considers any and all benefits. articles.title: LeBron James and Will Smith the stars as Angola aims to cash in on E1 powerboat racing
articles.summary: Angola hopes hosting the E1 Series will boost tourism after NBA star LeBron James attends the inaugural powerboat race in the capital Luanda.
articles.body:
It is difficult to imagine an electric powerboat racing series capturing the attention of an Angolan audience for whom football and basketball is king, but the presence of NBA royalty LeBron James certainly helped.

The 41-year-old was among the A-listers in Luanda as the E1 World Championship rolled into southern Africa for the first time at the weekend, having made its debut on the continent last year in Lagos, Nigeria.

"It's not a short trip, but he [LeBron] is here because he believes in what we're doing," E1 chief executive Jamie Copas told BBC Sport Africa in the Angolan capital.

"You can't underestimate the value of it. They [the celebrity owners] come with huge followings."

Similar to Formula E on land, it aims to blend sport with strong messaging around sustainability and green technology.

James said Angola had made his first trip to the country "super welcoming" after visiting the National Museum of Slavery.

"Obviously there is a lot of history here," the new signing for the Philadelphia 76ers told local media.

"A lot of history that not only is here in the country but also [crosses] over to America."

Angola's men are reigning African basketball champions, securing a record-extending 12th continental title on home soil last year, and unsurprisingly spectators of the E1 racing at the Clube Naval de Luanda clamoured for a glimpse of one of basketball's biggest icons.

Journalist Omar Prata, covering the race for the Jornal de Angola, admitted that E1 was not on his radar until Hollywood star Smith, whose Westbrook Racing team is sponsored by Visit Angola, announced in March that a deal had been agreed to race in Luanda for the next three years.

"I see the potential it could bring to project the city at a time when the government is trying to work on tourism," Prata said.

"And of course it means a lot to have LeBron James here. Angolans have seen him on television, they try to emulate him on the street courts, they have his posters."

The star power of E1's owners is helping to bring eyeballs to what is a traditionally niche sport where powerboat pilots skim and bounce around tight courses at speeds close to 100kmph.

Yet, on a calendar that features traditional celebrity haunts like Miami, Monaco and Lake Como, Luanda's name seems an outlier.

Among those taking in the action from the fanzone was local resident Edson Cabeta.

"It is the first time I have seen anything like this," he said.

"Today it is foreigners doing this; tomorrow, perhaps we could have an Angolan team."

The aspiration is that hosting an E1 race will help Angola boost visitor numbers, with minister for tourism Marcio de Jesus Lopes Daniel saying enhanced foreign awareness of the country is the "first step" in a long-term plan.

"Our ambition is not simply to make Angola famous," Daniel told the BBC.

"It is to make Angola more desirable to visit, invest in and do business in."

Angola has not been afraid to speculate to accumulate in the past, bringing Lionel Messi's Argentina side to Luanda for a football friendly last November to celebrate 50 years of the nation's independence.

Daniel said it would be "premature" to assess the economic impact of this weekend's race in Luanda.

"An event of this scale generates demand across several sectors and it creates opportunities," he added.

"We want to turn the international attention generated by E1 into future trips, stays, private investment and jobs. That is the real return we are looking for."

Beyond the spectacle and waterfront backdrops, E1 aims to transcend motorsport.

Sustainability has been one cornerstone, and marine conservation efforts around the race in Angola included mangrove restoration.

Putting sustainability front and centre inevitably invites scrutiny - particularly when races have taken place in Saudi Arabia, the United States, Nigeria and now Angola, all major oil-producing nations.

"We're welcomed in places that do have a lot of fossil-fuel infrastructure.

"Each one of those markets is conscious of it and wants to be doing more from a green point of view. If we can help, why wouldn't we?"

Copas told BBC Sport Africa that E1 would only consider air freight as a last resort for transporting its teams and that they aim to showcase their technology on each stop, persuading people that electric charging is a viable alternative to diesel even on water.

But as the global series expanded to 10 teams and seven races in 2025, its own emissions rose from 1,672 tonnes of carbon dioxide equivalent in its first season to 4,049 tonnes in its second, according to E1's own annual sustainability report.

"We need to travel to meet new people, to tell our stories, which we would hope would be of greater benefit than the carbon footprint that we have," Copas explained.

"We work really hard to offset our carbon and to make sure every stage of our logistics journey is done in the most sustainable way.

"It would be crazy for us to say we're not going to travel and we're not going to race, because then we can't do the job that we're here to do."

There is an acknowledgement within E1 that the work is unfinished and that more active reductions are needed.

E1 was due to return to Lagos in October, but Nigeria's race was cancelled earlier this month, perhaps showing how the series is still working to establish itself.

It means its longer-term impact in Africa will take time to judge, but the effect of its celebrity owners was obvious around the paddock in Luanda.

After visiting his pilots, Will Smith stopped for selfies and handshakes with fans, telling the crowd it was "great to be here".

On the water, however, there was no fairytale result as Westbrook Racing's hopes of victory were ended by a mechanical fault, with Team Brady taking the inaugural Luanda title.

Smith could have used the help of Kianda, the mermaid-like Angolan water spirit traditionally regarded as a protector of fishermen.

It will take one of her miraculous interventions if electric powerboat racing is to usurp football or basketball in Angolan affections, but Copas hopes E1 can leave a different legacy.

"I think it's for us to help tell Angola stories, and for Angola to help tell ours.

"We will be back next year, we will be back the year after. It's not just about what we're doing in the few days we're here.

"We'd love to see the journey they're on develop even more, and us playing a part in that."

articles.title: FCC Chairman Brendan Carr accuses James Talarico of running a 'hoax' over equal time statute
articles.summary: Brendan Carr accuses James Talarico of running a "hoax" by banking on public confusion over the equal time statute to drive clicks and donations.
articles.body: Federal Communications Commission (FCC) Chairman Brendan Carr accused Democratic Texas Senate candidate James Talarico of banking on public confusion over the equal time statute to drive clicks and donations. Last week, Talarico appeared on ABC’s "Jimmy Kimmel Live!," but the liberal late-night host insisted the interview had to air on YouTube, instead of broadcast television, because the FCC has "threatened" the network. The White House previously said Kimmel was "play-acting," because the FCC did not threaten him regarding interviewing Talarico, or any other candidate. Carr responded on Saturday to an account on X that complained Talarico was relegated to YouTube, but Sen. Ted Cruz, R-Texas, was allowed to appear on ESPN’s "College Gameday." The chairman blasted Talarico, noting that the equal time statute doesn’t apply to ESPN and does not prohibit anyone from interviewing anyone on broadcast TV. KIMMEL REVEALS HE'S INTERVIEWING JAMES TALARICO UNDER 'UNUSUAL CIRCUMSTANCES,' CITING FCC THREATS "It is about more speech, not less. Congress wanted to ensure that voters would decide elections, not media gatekeepers picking winners and losers by providing preferential airtime to some candidates and not others. Indeed, when the statute applies, it simply requires broadcast stations to offer comparable time and placement. And comparable does not necessarily mean an interview by the same person on the same program either," Carr wrote. "This ties back to Talarico," Carr continued. "He’s just running the same hoax he did a few months ago on Colbert for the purpose of getting clicks and donations — he’s banking on people not understanding the statute or operating as partisan lemmings." DEMOCRATIC REP TELLS ABC, CBS TO 'GROW A SPINE' AFTER KIMMEL ANNOUNCES ALTERNATIVE TALARICO INTERVIEW Former late-night host Stephen Colbert interviewed Talarico in February, ahead of the Texas Senate primary, in which he was competing against Texas Rep. Jasmine Crockett. Colbert's show, which has since been canceled, did not air the interview with Talarico and only posted it to the show's YouTube channel in February. Colbert announced at the time that CBS had stopped them from airing the interview. articles.title: In 2010, Anderson Cooper paid $4.3 million for a 1906 New York firehouse; he restored its historic exterior and turned the 8,240-sq-ft building into a home while preserving its fire pole
articles.summary: News News: When Anderson Cooper bought a historic former fire patrol house in New York’s Greenwich Village for $4.3 million in 2010, the purchase raised concerns.
articles.body: When Anderson Cooper bought a historic former fire patrol house in New York’s Greenwich Village for $4.3 million in 2010, the purchase raised concerns among local preservationists, according to contemporary reporting by DNAinfo and the Village Preservation Society. The four-storey building at 84 West 3rd Street had spent decades as a working Fire Patrol station, and its history was tied not only to New York’s firefighting past but also to one of the city’s most painful chapters: the September 11 attacks. Today, the 8,240-sq-ft property has been transformed into Cooper’s private home. Yet its historic identity has not disappeared. Cooper restored the building’s distinctive exterior, while elements of the former fire patrol house, including its original fire poles, were retained inside. The building was later protected as part of the South Village Historic District.A firehouse that wasn’t part of the FDNYBuilt in 1906 and designed by architect Franklin Baylies, Fire Patrol House No. 2 was not an ordinary New York firehouse. It belonged to the New York Fire Patrol, a privately funded service established by insurance companies to respond to fires and, importantly, protect buildings and their contents from damage caused by fire and water.The institution had roots stretching back to the early 19th century and predated New York’s municipal fire department. By the early 2000s, the New York Fire Patrol was the last operating insurance-supported firefighting organisation of its kind in the city. But in 2006, the service was disbanded and its properties were put up for sale.That triggered a preservation campaign. Village Preservation, then known as the Greenwich Village Society for Historic Preservation, had been pushing for the 84 West 3rd Street building to receive landmark protection, concerned that a private buyer could eventually alter or demolish it.Cooper’s purchase raised fears, then changed the storyCooper’s purchase initially worried preservationists and former fire patrol officers. The concern was straightforward: what would happen to a historic firehouse once it became a private home? Instead, the building underwent a major interior renovation while its distinctive historic character was retained. Village Preservation later described Cooper as having kept the building’s character intact while adapting it for residential use.The preservation battle also ultimately had a successful ending. The property was determined eligible for the State and National Registers of Historic Places in 2010. In 2013, it became part of the South Village Historic District, giving the building formal landmark protection.Its most poignant connection is to 9/11Perhaps the most remarkable chapter in the building’s history involves Keith Roma, a member of Fire Patrol No. 2. Roma, 27, had worked at the station for six years, following his father Arnold, who had also served with the Fire Patrol. On September 11, 2001, members of the patrol rushed to the World Trade Center alongside other first responders.Roma entered the North Tower repeatedly, helping people escape. He ultimately died at the World Trade Center and was the only New York Fire Patrol member killed there that day. His remains were recovered on Christmas Eve, 2001. Because the New York Fire Patrol was not part of the FDNY, Roma is not included in the official figure of 343 FDNY firefighters killed on 9/11. The State of New York, however, lists him among its fallen firefighters as a Fire Patrol member who died at the World Trade Center.From working firehouse to protected homeMore than a century after it was built, 84 West 3rd Street has undergone a remarkable transformation. What was once a working station for an almost forgotten private firefighting service is now a home, but one whose exterior and architectural identity remain protected. The fire pole, preserved amid the transformation, offers perhaps the simplest reminder of what the building once was: a place where firefighters lived, worked and answered calls long before it became one of New York’s most unusual celebrity homes.Ready to Make a Smarter Property Decision? articles.title: Bob Mackie dead at 87: Legendary fashion designer for Cher and Diana Ross dies
articles.summary: Legendary fashion and costume designer Bob Mackie, whose sequined gowns for Cher, Diana Ross, Tina Turner and other stars dazzled red carpets for decades, has sewn his final stitch.
articles.body: Legendary fashion and costume designer Bob Mackie, whose sequined gowns for Cher, Diana Ross, Tina Turner and other stars dazzled red carpets for decades, has sewn his final stitch. Mackie died Monday at 87, according to a post on his Instagram account. “He lived his 87 years to the fullest, fulfilling his dream of being a Fashion and Costume Designer, which is all he ever wanted to do,” the post read. “His genius and extraordinary designs will live on forever, continuing to bring beauty into this world.” His longtime publicist Jenelle Hamilton confirmed that he died of pneumonia on Monday morning in Palm Springs, Calif. Known as the “sultan of sequins,” Mackie dressed some of Hollywood’s biggest names over more than 50 years. His creations for celebrities like Carol Burnett, Liza Minnelli and Barbra Streisand stunned both performers and fans alike, and remain some of the most iconic costumes ever worn. “Every time I put something on that Bob made, I felt very, very special,” Sir Elton John said on social media Monday. “His costumes were works of art, and he will go down as one of the most legendary designers ever in Hollywood.” “He loved glamour like I love glamour, but more than anything, we shared the same sense of humour and had so much fun together,” he added. Born in the Los Angeles suburb of Monterey Park, Mackie first attended nearby Pasadena City College before transferring to what would become the California Institute of the Arts, the New York Times reported. He dropped out to work as a costume sketch artist in 1961, which included sketching the skintight, beaded dress worn by Marilyn Monroe in 1962 when she sang “Happy Birthday” to President John F. Kennedy. A year later he was hired by the man who would become his lifelong romantic and creative partner, Ray Aghayan, to work on “The Judy Garland Show.” The pair went on to win the first-ever Emmy Award for costume design in 1967. Aghayan died of kidney failure in 2011 at 83. Mackie was briefly married to Marianne Nicholson, an actress known as Lulu Porter and they divorced in the early 1960s, according to the Times. Their son, Robert Gordon Mackie Jr., who worked as a makeup artist, died from complications related to AIDS in 1993. His work with actress, singer and dancer Mitzi Gaynor in 1966, caught Burnett’s attention, according to a short biography on his website. Her producer hired him to design the complete wardrobe for “The Carol Burnett Show,” a post he held for 11 seasons. A star was born. “Throughout his extraordinary body of work, Bob Mackie understood the unique power of costume in comedy — to help create a character and become part of the creative energy that drove the comedy itself,” National Comedy Center Executive Director Journey Gunderson said in a statement. His work with Burnett, Cher, Joan Rivers, Bette Midler and Lucille Ball “helped shape some of comedy’s most memorable moments on television and stage,” he added. In 1982, Mackie launched a ready-to-wear collection and a line of collectable Barbie dolls, which featured red carpet-ready dresses complete with headdresses, dramatic long trains and his signature sequined glow. Throughout the decades, his designs took on an increasingly universal appeal despite — or perhaps because of — their sheer scale and luminosity. One of his most famous pieces, the flame dress, has been worn by pop icons Beyoncé and Turner, as well as Cher, with whom he also shared a lengthy creative partnership. The dress, a version of which first debuted in 1968 on “The Fred Astaire Show,” initially featured large gold paillettes. By the time Cher and Turner donned matching versions on “The Sonny & Cher Show,” the paillettes were replaced by smaller sparkly sequins that came to typify his work. The racy design was more of a bodysuit than a dress, with sheer nude cutouts and sequins sewn into the shape of flames. “A woman who wears my clothes is not afraid to be noticed,” Mackie famously once said. In 1986, after Cher was snubbed for her performance in “Mask,” Mackie outfitted her in a tall black feather headdress and beaded two-piece ensemble baring her famously toned midriff. Cher joked at the Academy Awards that at least she received her “Academy booklet on how to dress like a serious actress.” In 1999 he won an Emmy for “Cher: Live in Concert from Las Vegas” and another in 2003 for “Cher: The Farewell Tour,” according to the biography on his website. In total, Mackie won nine Emmy Awards and earned three Oscar nods over the course of his illustrious career. He was nominated for 30 Emmys. “With his choice of vibrant colors, luxurious fabrics, and intricate detail,” his website reads, “Bob Mackie’s work continues to exude timeless glamour.”

articles.title: How IAF achieved 314 km ‘longest kill’ of Pak aircraft during Op Sindoor, reveals MoD report
articles.summary: News News: NEW DELHI: The defence ministry’s annual report 2025-26, released on Sunday, recorded what it described as the “longest surface-to-air kill” — of a “P.
articles.body: NEW DELHI: The defence ministry’s annual report 2025-26, released on Sunday, recorded what it described as the “longest surface-to-air kill” — of a “Pakistani special-mission aircraft by an Indian S-400 unit from a distance of 314 km”, during Operation Sindoor and also provided details of several key IAF targets in Pakistan, including fighter aircraft hangars, runways and command-and-control centres.Explaining the longest kill, the report said, “Indian radars tracked the threat in silence and through flawless precision, the long range surface-to-air missile was guided through its far boundary. This crucial operation proved to the adversary that no point on ground or in air was beyond the reach of IAF offensive elements.”Though the defence ministry's 2025 report did not identify the Pakistan aircraft, there were reports earlier that India shot down a Pakistani Saab 2000 AEW&C/ELINT (Airborne Early Warning and Control / Electronic Intelligence) aircraft from the Russian-acquired S400. India currently has in its possession four S-400 squadrons out of the five contracted under the 2018 deal with Russia, with three already operational and the fifth is expected by Nov.“With this operation, IAF rewrote the rules of air defence and the belief of the enemy that distance could provide it with protection was challenged," the report said.After the operation, India has undertaken a comprehensive review of capability voids with clear focus on force restructuring, enhancing jointness and integrating emerging technologies.During Op Sindoor, IAF carried out precision strikes on terror infrastructure across Pakistan, targeting locations such as Nur Khan and Rahimyar Khan air bases. The IAF also played a critical role in protecting Indian airspace during retaliatory drone and UAV attacks. A layered air defence grid, including the indigenously developed Akash missile system along with Pechora and OSA-AK platforms, was deployed effectively. The integrated air command and control system enabled real-time coordination, helping neutralise aerial threats and sustain net-centric operations throughout the conflict, the report said.The report also talked about the situation within J&K and along the Line of Control (LC), which had significantly altered during Op Sindoor. However, after the Director Generals of Military Operations (DGsMO)-level talks on May 10 and 12, 2025, the situation stabilised to a large extent, though the unpredictability continues, it said. In terms of infiltration bids in 2025, six such attempts were made by terrorists. Twelve Pakistani terrorists were neutralised while attempting infiltration along the LoC.While there is a decline in the frequency of infiltration along the LC as compared to previous years, it is assessed that infiltration attempts by terrorists are more focussed towards the International Border (IB) sector to include smuggling of narcotics and war-like stores. As compared to two ceasefire violations (CFVs) along LoC during 2024, 163 CFVs (124 CFVs during Op Sindoor) were recorded in 2025.

articles.title: Immigrants held in small outdoor cages at 'Alligator Alcatraz' in Florida, investigators find
articles.summary: DHS inspectors say they found the immigration-detention centre violated basic standards for hygiene, medical care, food and safety.
articles.body:
Immigrants held at "Alligator Alcatraz", a now-shuttered detention centre in Florida, were kept in small metal cages for hours, according to a report from the US Department of Homeland Security's watchdog.

The Office of the Inspector General (OIG) found the use of the outdoor cages - about 18sq ft (1.67sq m) - was "unprecedented among detention facilities" and dangerous.

Investigators concluded the centre also did not comply with a number of standards for hygiene, medical care, food, health and safety.

The BBC has contacted DHS's Immigration and Customs Enforcement (ICE) and Florida Governor Ron DeSantis for comment. DHS told the watchdog that state officials ran the facility.

In its response included in the investigation report, DHS officials said Florida - not the federal government - had authority over day-to-day operations at the facility.

The facility was established by the state of Florida through an executive order signed by DeSantis, but the federal government paid for operational costs.

In January, the OIG conducted a surprise inspection at the detention facility, which had become one of the most notorious immigration detention centres in the US. The OIG is an independent internal watchdog at DHS. The current inspector general was appointed by President Donald Trump during his first term.

In 2025, the detention facility was built over the course of eight days in the Everglades, a protected wetland known for its alligators. Trump once joked that immigrants held there would need to learn "how to run away" from the reptiles at the facility, which civil rights groups have decried as inhumane.

In June 2026, DeSantis said the facility would close as it was only meant to be temporary.

According to the OIG report, between July 2025 and January 2026, the facility kept 79 immigrants in the small metal enclosures, describing them as "calming areas" for people to "deescalate and have time alone". They were held there from periods ranging from minutes to nearly two hours, at least once as a disciplinary measure, OIG said.

"The use of such restrictive spaces is highly unconventional and does not align with standards for humane treatment," the report stated.

Detainees at the facility have previously told the BBC they were denied necessary medication and regular showers and other hygiene measures.

In their report, OIG inspectors said they found immigrants held at the facility had to use showers infested with small bugs and were only allowed to do so three times a week.

The facility did not provide them with sufficient living space, "creating cramped conditions for detainees who spent most of their time in their housing units", according to the report.

Immigrants at the centre also told OIG that they did not have access to clean drinking water and could not clean the plastic cups from which they drank.

articles.title: Government set to nationalise troubled steel firm, minister says
articles.summary: Production at SSUK sites in South Yorkshire and the West Midlands was paused earlier this year.
articles.body:
A plan to nationalise the UK's third-largest steelworks is being developed by the government, MPs have been told.

Business Secretary Jonathan Reynolds told the House of Commons ministers were looking to acquire Speciality Steel UK (SSUK), which has sites in Stocksbridge and Rotherham in South Yorkshire and Wednesbury in the West Midlands.

The government initially took control of SSUK, previously part of Liberty Steel, last year after it was forced to liquidate by the High Court.

Reynolds said a bidder had come forward earlier this year, but the government had decided against supporting it, citing "serious concerns" over the proposed financing of the deal and "protections for UK taxpayers".

Ministers had therefore decided that the government would plan its own formal acquisition of the business, he explained.

Production at the business, which employs about 1,300 people, was paused several months ago, with staff put on furlough on reduced wages.

Reynolds told the Commons: "Having concluded that we cannot support the preferred bidder's proposal, we are faced with a choice.

"We can allow events to take their course through the liquidation process and risk being left with no say in the future of these sites, or we can act.

"We will therefore engage with the official receiver sale process and develop a proposal for the public acquisition of SSUK.

"This will preserve strategic control and ensure that all credible future opportunities can be properly considered before irreversible decisions are taken."

Future decisions and spending commitments relating to the business would be "subject to detailed due diligence and funded from existing government budgets", Reynolds said.

He added: "Working towards public acquisition will create the necessary time and space to undertake a full assessment of the opportunities available.

"It will let us consider future industrial use, regeneration opportunities and the role that specialist manufacturing capabilities could play in supporting growth and our national resilience."

In a message to workers, he said: "I will do all I can to secure a bright future for you, your communities and your families."

articles.title: Richard Tice apologises for not declaring Israel trip during debate
articles.summary: The visit, funded by Reform Friends of Israel, was declared in his register of interests but not during the debate.
articles.body:
Reform UK's deputy leader Richard Tice has apologised in the House of Commons for failing to declare a trip to Israel during a debate on pro-Israel influence on UK politics.

The MP for Boston and Skegness said he did not mention the visit, which was funded by Reform Friends of Israel, during a speech he made in a Westminster Hall debate on 22 June.

Although the trip was recorded in his register of interests, Tice acknowledged he should have declared it during his speech.

The parliamentary commissioner for standards has been investigating whether Tice broke rules requiring MPs to be "open and frank in declaring any relevant interest" during debates in Parliament.

The visit to Israel took place between 26 and 30 September 2025 and was declared in Tice's register of interests on 19 October 2025.

According to the register , the trip cost an estimated £6,250, covering flights, accommodation, transport and hospitality for two people.

It states that Tice met Israel's foreign minister and president during the visit.

Tice told MPs: "Whilst the trip is properly recorded in my register of interests I should have declared it during the speech. That is a breach of the rules and I apologise to this good House."

Rule 6 of the parliamentary code of conduct says: "Members must always be open and frank in declaring any relevant interest in any proceeding of the House or its committees, and in any communications with ministers, members, public officials or public office holders."

The parliamentary commissioner for standards opened an investigation into whether Tice had failed to declare an interest on 28 July, with the inquiry extended on 20 August.

The commissioner has not yet published his decision and the inquiry is ongoing.

articles.title: Pontypool-born actor Luke Evans survived Hollywood by listening to actors he admired
articles.summary: The star discusses his "emotional connection" to his character in a new ITV drama, The Party.
articles.body:
Actor Luke Evans said he has survived Hollywood by "watching and listening" to actors he admired.

Pontypool-born Evans made the observation while discussing his similarities and "emotional connection" to his character in a new ITV drama, The Party.

It will see Evans star as Martin Gilmour, a journalist shaped by his lifelong friendship with a wealthy and charismatic politician played by Aberystwyth-born Tom Cullen.

The thriller moves between the birthday party of Cullen's character, Ben Fitzmaurice, and a police investigation that follows.

Evans, who is also an executive producer of the five-part series, said he drew on his own experiences to play the character.

"I think that's probably why I resonated with the story when I read the book," Evans said of the novel the series, which is based the book written by Elizabeth Day.

"Watching and listening is how I've managed to survive this industry.

"If I'm on a film set, I'm always watching other actors or older actors that I've been admiring for years," he added.

Evans said this trait of watching others was something he shared with Gilmour, who he said he connected with on a "very deep level".

"It's not always possible when you play a role that you can pull on your own personal life or experiences.

"In this role I definitely could, even when Martin chooses completely different life choices to ones I would make in his position," he said.

Evans described the programme as a "gripping exploration of loyalty, class and the truths we hide", describing Gilmour as a "very complex, deep, fascinating and tragic character".

"Every time I looked at him on the page, I discovered something more. He's not somebody that broadcasts his feelings. He's suppressed them for such a long time."

articles.title: Judge Adam Levy previews his ‘nitty-gritty’ new show  – and how his style compares to his mom Judge Judy
articles.summary: Judge Adam Levy says he "learned from the best" as his mom Judge Judy Sheindlin created "Adam's Law," premiering Sept. 14 in national syndication.
articles.body: STAMFORD, CT — Judge Adam Levy’s new courtroom show "Adam’s Law" premieres this month, and he feels prepared because he "learned from the best," his mom Judge Judy Sheindlin. Sheindlin’s popular show "Judge Judy" ran for over 25 years. She's now passing the baton to her son, who has also starred in courtroom shows like "Justice on Trial" and "Tribunal Justice." Before bringing his talents to television, Levy served two terms as Putnam County district attorney in New York. He was one of three adjudicating judges on "Tribunal," but he’ll be the lone judge at the helm for CBS Media Ventures' "Adam’s Law," premiering Monday. "Well, we dive into the nitty-gritty," Judge Adam Levy told Fox News Digital at Stamford Studios following a taping of the show this summer. JUDGE JUDY'S SON, FELLOW JUDGES DISH ON WHY AUDIENCES LOVE TV COURTROOM DRAMA: INSTANT ACCOUNTABILITY "We get into the details. The devil’s always in those details. And so we make sure that the information that we have isn’t just limited to what the litigants tell us in a complaint or an answer. When appropriate, we will look into backgrounds to ensure what they tell us is corroborated or if we can contradict it, we will. So the right person wins, the right person loses," he added. Two women became visibly emotional during the two cases Levy presided over that morning, sharing their testimonies through tears. While Levy said he understands that these are real people with feelings, he aims to focus on the facts and not the emotions. "The law is about facts," Levy said. "The law doesn’t have much to do with feelings. I tell that to my family all the time – my facts don’t care about your feelings. Listen, these are real cases, they’re real people. And many of them come here, and they’re committed to their cause. They feel strongly. The ones we had today were high-dollar values, but it could be a $50 case, it could be a $100 case, it doesn’t make a difference. JUDGE JUDY'S SON ADAM LEVY SAYS HE COULD FIX LOS ANGELES 'IN A MONTH' "The plaintiffs feel wronged, and they want justice. And when they really start getting emotional, you see that. You see that whatever happened to them really bothered them. I take their cases seriously. They come to us and waive their right to be heard in small claims court, and allow me to adjudicate the cases for them. Why would I give them anything less than my full attention and true justice?" Levy said he knew he was ready for his own show "when Judge Judy told me I was ready for my own show." "I was very happy to go back to Wyoming, going skiing, but it was time," he shared. "She wanted to reassess what she was doing, and thinking about maybe hanging up her gavel, and she felt as though it was time. It was time for me that I had developed whatever skills she thought were necessary…" "I don’t want to disappoint her," he joked. "I don’t want the word ‘bupkis’ next to my name in the will." Levy described his courtroom style as "similar" to his mom’s. "We both can’t stand nonsense," he said. "If you’re going to come in, and you’re going to lie, neither of us really have much tolerance for that, patience for it… Come to the court, tell the truth. A trial is supposed to be a search for the truth and not about who can tell a better lie. That’s what we’re all about." FORMER PROSECUTOR ADAM LEVY SENDS WARNING FOR KNICKS PARADE SAFETY AFTER NYC CHAOS Growing up, he admitted he didn’t always appreciate his mom's work schedule and his life as a latchkey kid as Judge Judy juggled her responsibilities. Now he admires her work ethic, saying she passed it down to him, and he hopes to do the same for his kids. Levy quipped that his kids think he's "crazy" because of the hours of prep he does each week for the show, but he wants to be prepared for the litigants who called him for help. "It’s much easier when you love what you do," he said. CLICK HERE TO DOWNLOAD THE FOX NEWS APP "Adam’s Law" was created by Judge Judy Sheindlin. It is produced by her Queen Bee Productions and premiered Monday in national syndication.

articles.title: Britain’s Devil’s Arrows came from Brimham Rocks 18 km away, revealing that prehistoric people deliberately moved the giant stones
articles.summary: UK News: Britain’s tallest surviving stone row may have travelled farther than archaeologists once believed, after scientists traced tiny mineral grains on its.
articles.body: Britain’s tallest surviving stone row may have travelled farther than archaeologists once believed, after scientists traced tiny mineral grains on its weathered surfaces to a distinctive rocky landscape 18 kilometres away. The Devil’s Arrows, a group of enormous prehistoric stones near Boroughbridge in North Yorkshire, have long been linked to a closer gritstone source. According to the new study published in The Royal Society, titled ‘Deliberate prehistoric sourcing of the Devil's Arrows, Britain's tallest stone row’, strips of adhesive tape were placed against the stones to recover mineral grains without damaging the protected monument. Dating 236 zircon grains has now produced a striking geological fingerprint, pointing towards Brimham Rocks rather than the nearer Plumpton Rocks.Peel method reveals hidden clues from the Devil’s ArrowsThe researchers needed a way to examine the Devil’s Arrows without taking conventional rock samples from the protected monument. They therefore used what the study describes as a novel “peel method”. Twenty-centimetre sections of adhesive tape were placed against dry, inconspicuous areas of the stones for five minutes, collecting tiny grains from their surfaces. The approach was carried out under Scheduled Monument Consent granted by Historic England.The material recovered from the three surviving stones was enough to produce 236 concordant zircon U–Pb dates. Stone 1 provided 67 ages, Stone 2 produced 64 and Stone 3 produced 105. Statistical tests found no significant difference between the zircon age patterns of the three stones, allowing the researchers to combine them into one dataset for comparison with potential source rocks.Zircon fingerprints link the Devil’s Arrows to Brimham RocksThe zircon record from the Devil’s Arrows contains several distinctive age groups, including dominant Palaeozoic grains dating to roughly 460–400 million years ago, alongside Mesoproterozoic grains from about 1.3–1.0 billion years ago and Palaeoproterozoic grains from around 1.8–1.5 billion years ago. There are also smaller Archean populations, with the oldest analysed grains reaching more than 3.7 billion years.When fingerprints were matched with potential source areas, Brimham Rocks produced the closest match. According to the study, the Devil’s Arrows and Brimham Rocks share the same broad polymodal zircon pattern and similar proportions of the different age groups. The statistical comparison was particularly strong with a Kolmogorov–Smirnov test, while Plumpton Rocks showed a substantially different zircon spectrum.Plumpton Rocks ruled out as the Devil’s Arrows’ likely sourcePlumpton Rocks has long been considered a possible source because it is nearer to the Devil’s Arrows and has the appropriate Millstone Grit lithology. The study notes that it is the source named in the Historic England Official List entry. Yet the mineral evidence tells a different story: the zircon population from Plumpton Rocks differs from both the monument and Brimham Rocks.The researchers explain that even outcrops belonging to the same Upper Plumpton Grit interval can have different mineral fingerprints because sediment was carried through separate ancient river channels. In their statistical comparison, the Devil’s Arrows had a much closer relationship with Brimham Rocks than with Plumpton Rocks, supporting Brimham as the more likely source.Why prehistoric people chose Brimham RocksThe researchers argue that the choice may have combined practical and cultural considerations. Brimham is a prominent tor landscape with unusual, weather-eroded rock formations, while natural joints and bedding planes create elongated blocks that could have made the lifting of large stones easier.There are also signs that Brimham itself was a place of prehistoric activity. The study points to a three-metre-long gritstone near the rocks carrying wavy engravings and around 21 cup-and-ring marks dating from the Late Neolithic to the Bronze Age. Taken together, the geological and archaeological evidence suggests that the Devil’s Arrows were not simply made from whatever suitable stone happened to be closest. As the researchers conclude, the monument represents an “intentional km-scale relocation” of material from a distinctive upland landscape into a lowland ceremonial setting.The Devil’s Arrows therefore add another example to evidence from monuments such as Stonehenge, Orkney and Irish passage tombs, where prehistoric communities transported stone over considerable distances. The new provenance evidence suggests that the people who raised the approximately seven-metre-high stones near Boroughbridge may have deliberately sought out.Catch the latest World News and Live updates. articles.title: EU states to raise game as Arctic becomes strategic geopolitical frontier
articles.summary: Europe racing Russia, China and US to seize security and economic opportunities.
articles.body:
European Union member states have agreed to increase investment in the Arctic amid a growing scramble for security advantages and vast natural resources.

Labelling the Arctic a “geopolitical hotspot”, a Monday meeting involving 12 countries called for the EU to “take on a more strategic and proactive role in the European Arctic”, meeting participants said in a joint statement.

The meeting, which featured the leaders of Finland, Denmark, Estonia, France, Greece, Germany, Latvia, Lithuania, the Netherlands, Poland, Romania and Sweden, focused on the race for influence over the Arctic as receding ice opens opportunities in the northern region. The discussion identified Russia as the largest threat to the European Arctic, but also noted the ambitions of China and the United States.

“This region has become a geopolitical hotspot,” German Chancellor Friedrich Merz told a news conference.

Despite Germany not being an Arctic country, Merz said his presence at the summit testified to the importance of the region to overall European security and suggested years of relative neglect should end.

“Let me put it this way: High north – and low attention – is over,” he said.

Russia, Canada, Iceland, Norway and the United States are considered Arctic countries, in addition to EU members Finland, Sweden and Denmark.

All have become involved in increasing geopolitical competition over the region as the retreat of ice sheets – spurred by climate change – has exposed its security and economic opportunities.

Russia has beefed up its military presence in recent years, reopening and modernising bases abandoned since the Soviet Union collapsed.

“Russia poses the most significant and long-term threat to Arctic security and stability. In order to respond to the threat posed by Russia, the EU must treat the Arctic as a strategic frontier,” said Finnish Prime Minister Petteri Orpo after the meeting.

The warming climate is opening up the Arctic for shipping, fishing, drilling and mining. China has made no secret of its interest in the territory, which is rich in natural resources.

The race has also stirred tension among NATO allies. Greenland, which is not part of the EU but overseen by Denmark, has become a bone of contention between the EU and the United States, with US President Trump claiming that Denmark cannot protect the Arctic island from Russia and China.

“I think everybody recognised that Greenland has been under a big pressure,” said Danish Prime Minister Mette Frederiksen.

Last week, the European Union signed a declaration with Greenland, promising a stronger partnership and announcing a 200-million-euro ($232m) investment package to soothe anxiety caused by repeated threats from Trump to annex the self-governing territory.
