articles.title: 23-year-old Georgia mayor removed from office after city alleges improper contact with teen, misuse of funds
articles.summary: Lawmakers in an Atlanta suburb removed the city’s young mayor, accusing him of misusing a municipal credit card and engaging in inappropriate, sexually explicit communications with a teenager, officials said Sunday.
articles.body: Lawmakers in an Atlanta suburb removed the city’s young mayor, accusing him of misusing a municipal credit card and engaging in inappropriate, sexually explicit communications with a teenager, officials said Sunday. The City Council of Stockbridge, Georgia, voted 3-0 to remove Jayden Williams, 23, from office about 10 months after he was elected. The city of nearly 30,000 people is about 20 miles southeast of Atlanta. “The City of Stockbridge confirms that the City Council has taken formal action concerning the Office of Mayor following proceedings conducted pursuant to applicable City processes,” according to a city statement on Sunday. “As a result of that action, the Mayor has been removed from office.” The city hired a law firm to investigate allegations against the youngest mayor in Stockbridge history. The probe found that, late last year, Williams flirted with and exchanged explicit images of himself with a high school student who had just turned 18. The two had been chatting electronically, via text and Instagram instant messages, about the student joining Williams’ mentorship program. When presented with text messages and evidence of these photos, Williams confirmed he had exchanged nude pictures. Williams had earlier told a local reporter that he didn’t remember whether he had ever exchanged illicit images with this young man. “Is getting nude photographs via text message so unremarkable to you that you don’t remember when you get them?” lawyer Robbie Ashe, representing investigators, asked then-Mayor Williams during a marathon council meeting on Saturday. Williams insisted that sharing such material is commonplace for younger Americans. “It’s not memorable nor is it abnormal for somebody my age,” he said. “That’s not abnormal for somebody my age.” The city now has six months to schedule a special election for the position, according to acting Mayor Elton Alexander. “Removing Stockbridge Mayor Jayden Williams from office was a tough decision; it brings a fair and equitable close to multiple troubling accusations,” Alexander said in a statement. Williams could not be immediately reached by NBC News for comment on Monday. But a lawyer for Williams said the allegations against his client didn’t warrant removal from office. Attorney Robert Kenner also noted that any illicit communications with that young man happened in December last year, before his client took office. The former mayor also admitted to making improper purchases on his city-issued credit card, but claimed it was an accident — because the municipal card is the same color and looks similar to his personal card. The city has been reimbursed for those purchases, Williams said, and no criminal charges have been filed against him. “Tonight was very disappointing,” Kenner told reporters after the council meeting on Saturday night. “I don’t believe that it was based on any evidence.” Williams defeated incumbent Anthony Ford, 2,909 votes to 2,489 votes, or about 54.8% to 45.1% in November last year. Stockbridge operates under a city manager form of government so the mayor’s role is largely ceremonial. The mayor only votes on council business to break ties. “The City will continue to conduct municipal business and provide services to residents, businesses, and the community without interruption,” according to the city. “The City Manager, department leadership, and City employees will continue performing their respective duties in accordance with applicable law and City policies.” Alexander, the interim mayor, said he will not run for the job. “I have no desire to be mayor,” he told reporters on Saturday. “We have a council-manager form of government. What that means is the mayor’s position has very few powers in the city of Stockbridge. For me to run for mayor means giving up my ability to vote and I would never do that.”

articles.title: Farm tax a mistake, Lord Blunkett says in call for Burnham 'rural reset'
articles.summary: The former mentor to Prime Minister Andy Burnham has joined ex-PM Lord Cameron in criticising rural policies.
articles.body:
An inheritance tax for farms was "a mistake" and Andy Burnham should use his premiership to listen to the countryside more, his longtime mentor Lord Blunkett has said.

The former Labour minister hit out at "Treasury economic orthodoxy" over the 20% tax on inherited agricultural assets worth more than £2.5m that came into force in April, ending a waiver farms had since the 1980s.

He spoke at the launch of a new campaign by the Countryside Alliance for a "rural reset" to reverse what the group says is a current set of policies "treating rural people as the enemy".

The government said it was "determined to rebuild trust" with farmers and that most estates were unaffected by the tax hike.

The tax, announced in last year's Budget under Sir Keir Starmer at half the 40% rate of standard inheritance tax, was initially proposed for inherited agricultural assets worth more than £1m.

A backlash led to it being watered down in December - to a raised threshold of £2.5m.

Some rural campaigners say this still impacts ordinary working family farms and are calling for it to be scrapped.

Burnham has not hinted any change or U-turn on the issue, but Lord Blunkett said he was confident the now-prime minister, who he hired as his parliamentary private secretary back in 2004, would get the message "very clearly and act accordingly".

"I think the family tax, the family farm imposition, was a mistake," the former Labour minister said, adding it "touched a nerve".

"It's very strange because we've never won so many rural seats since 1945 - around 135 Labour MPs are either rural or semi-rural - and their voices need to be heard much more clearly," he told the BBC.

"If you're an urban dweller all your life and you've got Treasury economic orthodoxy in your soul, you won't understand that family farms are only family because they are passed down from one generation to another."

He said the countryside fits neatly into Burnham's self-professed focus on local postcodes and urban and rural areas "need each other".

Lord Blunkett also branded the government's planned ban on trail hunting a mistake, saying the practice was "doing no harm".

Trail hunting was introduced after the Hunting Act 2004 as an alternative to hounds chasing foxes and involves using an animal-scented rag. Labour first announced a planned ban in its 2024 election manifesto.

The government said there was strong support for a ban on trail hunting and that it posed risks to wildlife and pets.

Former Prime Minister Lord Cameron criticised both policies at a Countryside Alliance event in Westminster on Monday, calling the inheritance tax on farm assets "stupid" and the trail hunting ban "completely wrong".

Also taking aim at the government's call for evidence on game shooting in England, Lord Cameron warned further crackdowns risk eroding all facets of rural life including pubs and local services.

"Some of these things we should be angry about," he added, a week after being spotted filming an episode of Prime series Clarkson's Farm which has popularised various issues facing farmers.

The Countryside Alliance says its campaign is a non-political effort to encourage Burnham to work with rural people to address their concerns about policies on issues like farming, horseracing and greyhound racing.

Farmers have held tractor protests in parts of the country over the last year.

The government said: "This is the start of a new conversation with farmers and rural communities as we work together to build a stronger future for British farming and unlock growth in rural areas."

articles.title: India to supply Nepal electricity after floods wrecked hydropower projects
articles.summary: India to provide Nepal with 654 megawatts of electricity daily to meet urgent needs after devastating glacial floods.
articles.body:
India has approved the expedited export of electricity to neighbouring Nepal to help it overcome shortages caused by extensive damage to hydropower infrastructure from devastating floods last month.

In a statement on Monday, India’s Ministry of Power said up to 654 megawatts of electricity would be transmitted for 18 hours per day until December 31.

“The approval will help Nepal meet its power requirements during this difficult period and further strengthen the close and longstanding energy cooperation between India and Nepal,” it said.

It added that in December it would also review the amount of power to be exported from January.

The flooding , triggered on August 26 by a glacial mountain collapse on the China-Nepal border, killed more than 1,400 people in Nepal and Tibet.

At least 12 hydropower projects in Nepal were hit, with at least 900 power station workers among the more than 5,500 people still missing in the country.

Almost 100 percent of the country’s energy needs were met by hydropower before the floods hit. Since then, Nepal has been forced to import electricity after years of exporting surplus energy to India.

Thousands of displaced people are sheltering in aid centres, with little hope of returning home soon. The United Nations and its partners are appealing for nearly $50m to help survivors.

Nepali officials say at least $5bn is needed for initial rebuilding, adding that the disaster shows how climate change has hit poor countries that did little to cause it.

The ‌Himalayas, where Nepal is nestled, are approaching a tipping point as glaciers melt ⁠faster than a decade ⁠ago, threatening water security as the region approaches “peak water” by mid-century, according to a study released this month.

articles.title: How researchers use machine learning to re-create chirps and trills produced by forest insects when Dinosaurs lived on Earth
articles.summary: Tech News News: You must have heard the ancient insect sounds and songs in Steven Spielberg’s dinosaur movies wherein the trills and high-pitched chirps fill the prim.
articles.body: You must have heard the ancient insect sounds and songs in Steven Spielberg’s dinosaur movies wherein the trills and high-pitched chirps fill the primeval forests as characters move through large leaves and trees. While those sounds have been whipped up by Hollywood sound engineers, scientists are taking the help of technology for a different approach. They are using machine learning to reconstruct them straight from 165-million-year-old fossilised insect wings.According to a study published in the Proceedings of the National Academy of Sciences, an international team of researchers blended exceptionally preserved fossil remains, biomechanical tests on living species, digital simulations and machine learning models to resurrect a partial acoustic portrait of the Middle Jurassic period. If verified, one of the discovered signals stands as the earliest recorded evidence of ultrasonic animal communication which predates the rise of echolocating bats by tens of millions of years.Commenting on the paper, University of Denver behavioral ecologist Robin Tinghitella, who researches cricket evolution but was not part of the study, noted that listening to a hypothetical prehistoric soundscape generated directly from data is a compelling scientific milestone.How researchers decoded ancient sound from wing designAcoustic waves cannot turn to stone, but the specialised bone-and-cuticle structures that generate them do leave a fossil trail. Crickets and katydids (bush crickets) produce noise via stridulation. One forewing carries a serrated vein known as a “file,” studded with minuscule, toothlike ridges. Rubbing an opposing wing's scraper across this ridged file sets the wing membrane into rapid vibration. By measuring the exact physical spacing and length of these ridges alongside the wing's overall surface area, researchers can reliably determine an insect's acoustic frequency and pitch.The investigation centered on 20 distinct fossils spanning nine separate species discovered within the same geological horizon in modern-day Inner Mongolia. This shared environment gave scientists the opportunity to model a community of creatures that inhabited the very same prehistoric forest canopy.Scientists are validating models with lasers and machine learningTo translate flattened fossils into living audio, researchers developed biomechanical models and tested them against modern crickets and bush crickets. Using precision laser systems, they mapped how today's insect wings flex and resonate during song.Having checked the mechanical equations on existing species, the scientists then tested those parameters on fossilized wings. Machine learning algorithms were brought in to process the repetition rates, estimating how fast these extinct species rattled out their core sound pulses.The resulting audio profiles paint an unexpected picture of the ancient night. For example, most Jurassic species trilled in lower tonal registers similar to contemporary crickets. However, an extinct katydid relative called Sigmaboilus peregrinus emitted frequencies between 20 and 22 kilohertz, essentially crossing the boundary into ultrasound just outside normal human perception.Interestingly, rather than buzzing or rasping like some modern insects, many of these species produced narrowband pure tones that resemble sharp electronic beeps or clear, high-pitched whistles.Study co-lead Fernando Montealegre-Zapata, a sensory biologist at the University of Lincoln, explained that these concentrated musical frequencies make it exceptionally difficult for listeners to pinpoint where the noise originated—a vital defense mechanism against predators hunting in the dark.Montealegre-Zapata's team suggests that as early mammalian predators developed sharper hearing to track down calling insects, evolutionary pressures favoured cleaner, higher-frequency tones that shielded their positions.Get the latest technology news and updates. articles.title: Bill Maher says Californians will 'never vote for a Republican' as long as Trump is associated with the party
articles.summary: Maher argued California will never vote for a Republican as long as President Donald Trump is involved in the party, even as failures mount.
articles.body: Comedian and podcast host Bill Maher called out deep-blue California on Monday and said the state's voters would always support a Democrat, even if their policies were failing, as long as President Donald Trump was associated with the Republican Party. During an interview on "Club Random" with David Foster, Maher argued that California would never vote for a Republican as long as Trump was involved in the party. Maher noted Spencer Pratt, a Republican who finished third in Los Angeles' mayoral race and therefore did not advance to the general election, had the instinct that California had a "failed system," and Maher agreed. "It just shows that, in this state, I guess everywhere, we're so bipartisan now, that we will accept failure, which we plainly have here in California, over voting for the party of Trump," Maher said. "Which, I understand, because he does a lot of things that are I mean, plus, Jesus, I mean, I get a lot of s--- from him for the things I criticize just off the top of my head, vulgar, corrupt, doesn't concede elections, you know, inept at things that sometimes were a good idea to begin with. Close the border, you know, get rid of nuclear weapons in Iran, but f---ed up the execution." GAVIN NEWSOM AVOIDS QUESTION ON BRINGING BACK SAT SCORES AFTER UC OPEN LETTER, ASKS 'SHOW ME THE DATA' "As long as he's there, this state will never vote for a Republican, no matter how bad the Democrat gets. And that is a bad place to be," he continued. Psychotherapist and author Jonathan Alpert told Fox News Digital, "This isn't just a California or Democratic problem. Republicans can fall into the same trap. Once politics becomes part of your identity, it's remarkably easy to excuse things from your own side that you'd be furious about if the other side did them. That's the bigger problem Maher is getting at. If politicians know you'll vote for them no matter what, why should they be afraid of failing you?" Maher also compared government-run grocery stores to "what they looked like" in Cuba and the Soviet Union. TEXAS’ LARGEST SCHOOL DISTRICT SEES TEST SCORES SOAR AFTER STATE TAKEOVER DESPITE RACISM CLAIMS "I don't think we should have government-run grocery stores. I remember what they looked like in Cuba and the Soviet Union. It wasn't great. You know, kids, we tried this s---," Maher said. Both Foster and Maher said it "doesn't" work. Maher has been outwardly critical of California's policies, including education. He was critical of California Democrats during his "Real Time" show in July over education and green energy, arguing that Mississippi and Texas are outperforming the deep-blue state on issues Democrats often campaign on. MAMDANI’S CITY GROCERY PLAN COULD LEAVE TAXPAYERS PAYING FOR EVERY BANANA "Democrats, these are your issues: education, race, the environment," Maher said. "And I say this with love: you’re losing to the Waffle House, car-on-the-lawn states." Maher said California’s school outcomes were especially difficult to defend when compared with Mississippi, citing fourth-grade results for Black students. "Did you know that a Black fourth grader in Mississippi is 2.5 times as likely to be proficient in math and reading as one in California?" Maher asked. "Mississippi is kicking our a-- in education and for way less money. We’re 37th in fourth-grade reading. They’re ninth," he said. A Black Mississippi child is two and a half times as likely to be proficient in reading by fourth grade as a Black California child." The 2024 National Assessment of Educational Programs snapshots show Black fourth-graders in Mississippi at 19% proficient and 2% advanced in reading, compared with 7% proficient and 1% advanced in California. articles.title: How Ukraine’s futuristic war could get ‘much worse,’ according to ex-Google CEO
articles.summary: Ukraine’s battlefield “kill zones,” where leaving your bunker can mean death by Russian drone within minutes, look set to grow swiftly as the war drives breathtaking technological advancements, former Google CEO Eric Schmidt has warned.
articles.body: Ukraine’s battlefield “kill zones,” where leaving your bunker can mean death by Russian drone within minutes, look set to grow swiftly as the war drives breathtaking technological advancements, former Google CEO Eric Schmidt has warned. Schmidt, now CEO and executive chairman of rocket maker Relativity Space, is helping Ukraine fight a technological battle with the Kremlin that moves so quickly that weapons can lose their advantage within months. “The rate of innovation is faster than I’ve ever seen, and I work in tech,” Schmidt told Richard Engel, NBC News’ chief foreign correspondent. Schmidt previously chaired the U.S. National Security Commission on Artificial Intelligence and has advised the Pentagon. As Russia’s full-scale invasion of Ukraine stretches into its fifth year, Schmidt said Moscow is becoming better at developing and deploying new weapons, eroding an advantage Ukraine had relied on. “Historically, Ukraine was this small, really smart, really fast innovator, and the Russians were, if you will, big, slow, not very capable. That’s changed,” he said in an interview for the weekly global affairs podcast “The World with Richard Engel and Yalda Hakim.” The conflict has become a testing ground for drone warfare and thus the place for some of the technology’s latest advancements. From the Ukrainian towns now covered in anti-drone netting to the sites deep inside Russia vulnerable to attack from Kyiv, drones have become the war’s defining weapon. President Donald Trump, who during his election campaign promised to resolve the conflict in 24 hours, has repeatedly pressured Ukraine to cede key territory and favored Moscow’s hard-line demands. Winning would depend on how quickly either side could get its latest inventions into widespread use, Schmidt argued. “Whoever plays the game of fastest innovation to scale will win this war,” he said. Ukraine appears to agree with Schmidt’s assessment. The country’s new top general, Mykhailo Drapatyi, put innovation on a list of priorities he published after taking the position, saying Ukraine must learn faster than the enemy on the battlefield. President Volodymyr Zelenskyy has also recently noted the jet-powered Shahed drones problem, saying the Defense Ministry and the military must work on capabilities to intercept them. Schmidt expects artificial intelligence eventually to help computers direct drone swarms, using the results of attacks to improve how they fight. “Humans can’t run a swarm of 1,000 drones, but a computer can,” he said. “So what I think will happen is computers will develop war plans within a swarm.” For troops on either side, the drones already in use have made leaving cover dangerous. “The battlefield today is a no man’s land where nothing moves because there are drones and anti-drones above you,” he said. Small “first-person view,” or FPV, drones have become the war’s bullets, hunting exposed troops, Schmidt said. Russian aircraft also drop powerful glide bombs on Ukrainian positions, threatening soldiers who remain in their shelters. Russian troops are suffering heavy losses, too. Ukraine’s Defense Ministry estimates that 42,020 were killed or wounded in August, roughly 1,350 a day, following 42,860 in July. It described August’s toll as among the highest since the full-scale invasion began. Britain’s military chief, Air Chief Marshal Richard Knighton, said last week that Russia’s total casualties had reached 1.5 million, including approximately 500,000 dead. “The death rate on the Russia side is horrible. It’s just horrible, and these are human beings, too,” Schmidt said. Russia, meanwhile, has fitted some Iranian-designed Shahed attack drones with small, inexpensive Chinese jet engines, Schmidt said, making them faster than the interceptors Ukraine uses against them. “So how do you intercept a faster drone? Well, you have to add your own jet engine to the anti-drone,” he said. The jet-powered drones can reach a cruising speed of over 300 miles per hour, compared with a reported 110 miles per hour of older versions, according to the Open Source Munitions Portal, a weapons tracking project. Eight months ago, Ukrainian teams had been successfully countering Shaheds, he said. Now they are having to find ways to stop the faster versions. He argued that Western countries should be doing more to learn from Ukraine’s experience and help it respond. “How could we not be capturing this knowledge in the West to defend our own countries?” he asked. Ukraine is also competing for American weapons. In March, Zelenskyy told NBC News he feared the war with Iran could divert U.S. supplies to the Middle East, although he said scheduled deliveries to Kyiv had not been disrupted at that point. Schmidt warned the fighting could develop into “total war,” with Ukrainians determined to resist because they fear defeat would destroy their families. “Everything in both countries is a target for everything else. That’s just horrible,” he added. He also held out the hope that powerful computer systems might deter both sides from attacking, each unable to predict how the other would respond. “They need Western help,” he said of Ukraine. “In particular, they need some money, and they need technological help in order to counter this set of waves coming.” “If that help comes, I think Ukraine can hold.”

articles.title: Ella Langley, distractions and Lane Kiffin: Pete Golding calls Ole Miss-LSU ‘high school homecoming’
articles.summary: Pete Golding and Lane Kiffin remain friends but both want to call checkmate when LSU faces Ole Miss in one of college football's most hyped games.
articles.body: There will be moments on Saturday night in Oxford when it feels as though Lane Kiffin and Pete Golding are playing a game of chess against each other in a matchup that has been brewing for nine months. After a long offseason, and four games between both teams, the LSU Tigers will face Ole Miss in what has been the most discussed-talked-about game in recent memory. The young kids call it 'pure cinema' when describing a moment that takes place during a game that is built for a movie ending. When LSU gets off the bus on Saturday afternoon, the script will write itself on what should be one of the most insane atmospheres we will witness this season in college football. But, who is the pressure on? Is it Ole Miss, who has one of the more talented teams in the country, that faces the obstacle of making sure their jilted ex doesn’t come back into the house and steal a win? COLLEGE FOOTBALL’S CHAOS ERA IS HERE: TEXAS RALLIES, OREGON FALLS AND LANE KIFFIN EYES RETURN TO OLE MISS OLE MISS HAD FBI AGENT SWEEP FOOTBALL FACILITY FOR BUGS AFTER LANE KIFFIN LEFT FOR LSU Or, is it on Lane Kiffin to make his grand return to Oxford and lead his football team to a win over the group he left for LSU? "I told the players today, man, you don't have anything to worry about as far like attention on you all week," Kiffin said on Monday. "There's going to be so much attention, hatred, everything on me, you just get to go play. "I said, 'really, the pressure is on them (Ole Miss)'. They're the team that, we won seven games last year and they won thirteen. They return two Heisman candidates. How often has that ever happened in the same backfield? Second longest winning streak in the country. You guys just get to go play, and the pressure is not on you." That's certainly one way to look at this situation. No, the pressure is on both teams, with Kiffin and Pete Golding at forefront Let's be clear about this: both teams are under the gun with this game. For Ole Miss, this is about making sure that guy who left town for the perceived prettier girl doesn’t stroll back into town and rub your face in it. As for Lane Kiffin, he knows exactly how this buildup will play out. He's not only coaching football, but he's also selling tickets. Luckily for him, he's already accomplished that over the offseason, which started after he bolted Oxford for Baton Rouge before the Rebels started preparing for a college football playoff run. But, he will downplay the entire ordeal, which should be expected until sometime Friday afternoon when LSU starts their trek to northern Mississippi.
